h1:
Things to Do in Sing Buri
Temples, History & Nature
intro: Sing Buri is a small province just about 140 km from Bangkok, close enough for an easy out-and-back day trip, but it packs in a lot of stories: old Ayutthaya-era temples, the historic site of Bang Rachan Camp, and a quiet way of life along the Noi River. We've picked spots that were genuinely worth the trip, mixing temples, history and nature so you can plan it all in a single day.

blocks.html: When people think of Sing Buri, two things usually come to mind: the Bang Rachan heroes and boat noodles. But walk around the province and you'll find there's more to see than you'd expect — one of Thailand's largest reclining Buddhas, an enormous blessing-pose Buddha on the riverbank, a retro Thai market where people stroll in old warrior costumes, and rice fields and waterways that are perfect for an evening unwind. The best part is that the sights sit close together, so you can hit several on a single loop by car.

blocks.text: For temple lovers — old temples worth a stop

blocks.html: Sing Buri is a temple town, with several well-kept Ayutthaya-era monasteries that are still in active use. Pick three or four of the standouts and you'll have a full, satisfying day.

items.name: Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan
items.blurb: A royal monastery home to a giant reclining Buddha around 47 metres long, an old image crafted by Ayutthaya-era artisans. It's so long you have to step well back to take in the whole figure. The hall feels solemn and cool — a great place to start your trip.
items.meta: Mueang Sing Buri district · open roughly 6:00–18:00 · free entry

items.name: Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Yai)
items.blurb: Set on the bank of the Noi River, the highlight here is Phra Phuttha Suwan Mongkhon Maha Muni, or Luang Pho Yai — a large blessing-pose Buddha in gleaming gold that you can spot from afar. It's deeply revered by locals in Sing Buri, and plenty of people come to pray for blessings.
items.meta: Tha Chang district · on the Noi River · free entry

items.name: Wat Sawang Arom (Ban Bang Mon)
items.blurb: A temple of craftsmen, known for its Buddha-image sculpting and traditional Thai craft work. Inside there's a shadow-puppet (nang yai) museum showing antique leather-carving work — good for anyone who loves art and local craftsmanship.
items.meta: Ton Pho subdistrict, Mueang district · has a nang yai shadow-puppet museum

items.name: Wat Pho Kao Ton (Wat Mai Daeng)
items.blurb: An old Ayutthaya-era temple within the Bang Rachan Camp area, home to the hall of Phra Achan Thammachot, the spiritual leader of the Bang Rachan villagers. The temple sits right next to Bang Rachan Camp Park, so you can walk between the two in one spot — perfect for pairing with a bit of history.
items.meta: Khai Bang Rachan district · next to Bang Rachan Camp Park

blocks.title: Tip for temple-hopping
blocks.html: Temples in Sing Buri open early and stay quiet before 9 a.m. If you want clear photos of the Buddha images and cooler weather, start with Wat Phra Non Chaksi first thing in the morning — it's the most comfortable way to go.

blocks.text: For history buffs — the Bang Rachan heroes

blocks.html: The story of Bang Rachan Camp is the heart of Sing Buri. Villagers banded together and set up a camp to fight the Burmese army in the late Ayutthaya period, despite being far outmatched in numbers and weapons. They held out for several months, and their bravery became a legend. Coming here gives you both the story and the atmosphere that makes it clear why people across the whole country still remember the name Bang Rachan.

items.name: Bang Rachan Camp Park + Heroes' Monument
items.blurb: A leafy park with a cast-bronze monument of all 11 camp leaders, plus a museum building that tells the story of the battle. It's easy to wander and take photos, and a great way to bring kids face to face with history.

items.name: Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market
items.blurb: A market that recreates the old Bang Rachan village, with many visitors strolling in warrior costumes. There's food, sweets and souvenirs at fair prices, and riverside corners to rest. It's only open on certain days, so check before you go.

items.name: Ban Khu Mueang Ancient Town
items.blurb: An arboretum and archaeological site ringed by an ancient moat, shaded by large trees. Good for anyone who likes calm and history without the crowds.

blocks.text: For nature lovers — rivers and rice fields

blocks.html: Sing Buri has no mountains or waterfalls, but its charm lies in riverside life — the Chao Phraya River, the Noi River, and the Mae La River that's famous for its abundant fish. In the late afternoon, golden light falling over the rice fields and water is a lovely thing to sit and watch, and it's a perfect way to close out the trip.

items: Mae La Maharachanuson Park — on the fish-rich Mae La River, a relaxing spot to unwind and eat fresh freshwater fish, with quiet riverside rice-field surroundings.
Chao Phraya riverfront, town area — stroll along the embankment and watch local life and fishing boats. The evening breeze is just right, perfect for sipping a coffee.

Rice fields along the Bang Rachan road — driving between the temples and the park, you'll pass green paddies with several spots to pull over for photos, especially pretty in early rainy season when the fields turn deep green.

blocks.title: Good to know about the food
blocks.html: While you're in Sing Buri, don't miss Mae La snakehead fish and river prawns. The well-known spots are along the river and the Asia Highway, easy to fit in for lunch mid-trip.

blocks.text: How to make the most of a single day

blocks.html: Because the sights sit close together, a Sing Buri out-and-back day trip from Bangkok is easy to pull off. Having your own car is by far the most flexible option. Here's a route that flows nicely without backtracking.

items.activity: Start at Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan
items.note: See the giant reclining Buddha early when it's quiet and still cool

items.activity: On to Wat Phikun Thong to pay respects to Luang Pho Yai by the Noi River
items.note: Photograph the golden Buddha against the river view

items.activity: Into the Bang Rachan Camp area — Wat Pho Kao Ton + Bang Rachan Camp Park
items.note: Walk the two spots back to back and see the museum on the battle

items.activity: Lunch of Mae La snakehead fish / river prawns
items.note: Pick a riverside restaurant for the atmosphere too

items.activity: Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market (if it's an open day)
items.note: Snack as you stroll, buy souvenirs, photograph the retro corners

items.activity: Wrap up along the Chao Phraya River or at Mae La Park
items.note: Sit in the cool breeze and catch the sunset before heading back

blocks.title: About opening days
blocks.html: Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market only opens on certain days (usually Saturday–Sunday). If walking this market is the main reason for your trip, check the opening days on the market's page before you set off to be sure.

blocks.text: How to get to Sing Buri

items: Private car — from Bangkok, take the Asia Highway (Route 32) for about 140 km, roughly 2 hours. It's the most flexible way to loop around several sights.
Van / coach — there are services from Mo Chit and the new Southern terminal to Sing Buri town, but once there you'll need to hire local transport to reach the sights.
Combine with neighbouring provinces — Sing Buri borders Ang Thong, Lopburi and Chai Nat, so you can put together a smooth two-day trip linking the neighbours.

faq.q: What are the top things to do in Sing Buri?
faq.a: The standouts are Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan with its giant reclining Buddha, Wat Phikun Thong with the riverside Luang Pho Yai, and Bang Rachan Camp Park together with Wat Pho Kao Ton for history. If you like a retro vibe, add the Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market.

faq.q: Is one day enough for Sing Buri?
faq.a: Yes. The sights sit close together and most are around the town and Khai Bang Rachan district, so a single loop by car covers the temples, history and riverside spots in one day. It's well suited to an out-and-back trip from Bangkok.

faq.q: How far is Sing Buri from Bangkok, and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's about 140 km, around 2 hours by car via the Asia Highway (Route 32). There are vans and coaches to the town too, but having your own car makes hitting several sights much easier.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Sing Buri?
faq.a: It's a year-round destination. The late rainy season into early winter (October–February) brings comfortable weather and lush green rice fields. Come in early rainy season and you'll catch the paddies at their greenest.

faq.q: What's the best food in Sing Buri?
faq.a: It's known for Mae La snakehead fish, river prawns and boat noodles. The well-known spots are along the river and the Asia Highway, easy to fit in along your route mid-trip.
